The day after winning the prestigious Caine Prize award earlier in October, Kundizeza had told the BBC he was inspired after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho at an event in Ghana last year about her father's obsession with building fish tanks.
He said he had weaved that with fictionalised details from his own life around 2002 when Zimbabwe's economic troubles began.
Go to BBCAfrica.com for more news from the African continent.
Follow us on Twitter @BBCAfrica , on Facebook at BBC Africa or on Instagram at bbcafrica

title: Famed ship SS United States to be sunk off coast of Florida
content:
A ship that was once the fastest in the world and is longer than the Titanic will be sunk off the coast of Florida and turned into the world's largest artificial ocean reef.
The SS United States spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before it was moved to Florida, where it will soon become a home for sealife and an underwater attraction for marine enthusiasts.
Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner - which crossed the Atlantic Ocean hundreds of times - to be preserved as a museum.
Instead, after being purchased by a Florida county, it will be added to the dozens of artificial reefs off the coast, as a land-based museum detailing the ship's history is also planned.
Before its retirement, the SS United States was known for carrying royalty and celebrities from the US the Europe, beginning in 1952 and ending in 1969.
A young Bill Clinton, before he was president, used the ship to cross the Atlantic. Former presidents Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John Kennedy also travelled on the vessel.
The ship was moved from Philadelphia to Alabama last year for cleaning and remediation work. On Monday, it took its final journey from Alabama to the coast of Destin, Florida, where it will be sunk on Wednesday in a precision operation without explosives.
Stars including Marlon Brando, Coco Chanel, Duke Ellington, Salvador Dali, Walt Disney, Judy Garland and Cary Grant also boarded the ship during its sailing lifetime.
Before its purchase by the municipal Florida government, a number of proposals that would have seen the ship live a second life as a museum or a floating hotel failed.
Instead, the famed ship sat at various docks with various owners as legal battles played out.
The SS United States Conservancy group repeatedly attempted to keep the ship above water, but was unsuccessful.
Conservancy President Susan Gibbs - whose grandfather helped design the SS United States - said she was glad that the story of the ship would live on.
"[The ship] has always been this unabashedly American symbol that brings so many people together," Gibbs told CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

title: Author says there were 'real concerns' about David Walliams within publishing industry
content:
Author Chloe Combi has said she had heard rumours that there were "real concerns" about David Walliams's behaviour within the publishing industry more than a decade ago.
Combi told BBC News she had heard there were allegations about his "behaviour around young female staff" and says she was told in 2015 to warn schools that he was "not an appropriate booking".
An investigation by the Guardian and ITV News alleged that Walliams has been accused by several women of sexual misconduct, inappropriate behaviour and abusing his position, which he denies.
HarperCollins, which published Walliams's best-selling children's books, dropped Walliams last year after an investigation into his behaviour.
In response to the Guardian and ITV report, a spokesperson for HarperCollins said the company had decided not to publish any new titles by Walliams and that it took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously".
Walliams told ITV News and the Guardian that he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".
Combi said she was getting invited to events such as book launches around the time one of her own books was being published, and was also running a scheme to bring "high-profile and inspiring writers and speakers" to talk in schools.
At an event in 2015, Combi said she got speaking to someone "quite senior" in publishing, who warned her about Walliams.
"We were talking about [the scheme] and possible writers who might be good for the project to work well with teenagers," Combi said.
"She gave me some great recommendations and said to me: 'Whatever you do, don't invite David Walliams, and FYI if you are speaking to head teachers or teachers, please inform them that he's not a good booking, not an appropriate booking for a school'."
Combi continued: "I obviously asked why, and to be honest I had already heard quite a lot of rumours because those worlds are quite small and contained.
"One of the things she said was that there had been real concerns about his behaviour around young female staff."
Asked whether concerns about his behaviour was an open secret, Combi replied: "Yes definitely... and I'd heard it from people who worked in publishing, fellow writers, people kind of in celebrity and TV circles."
Combi said she never met Walliams herself, and said her information had come from "a number of people I was speaking to".
HarperCollins in September announced it would no longer be publishing his back catalogue.
The allegations against Walliams include:
In his statement to ITV News and the Guardian, Walliams said: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.
"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."
He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."
Earlier on Wednesday, media minister Ian Murray said there is a "cultural problem" in the industry that needs to be "stamped out".

title: Missing 11-month-old baby rescued after being buried alive in a crate in South Carolina
content:
An 11-month-old baby has been rescued in South Carolina after officials say he was buried alive in a crate by his father.
Koah Sharpe had been missing since Monday when he was taken by his father, Michael Comer, 25, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. Comer was arrested on a burglary charge on Monday evening but his son was not with him.
The baby was found on Tuesday "buried alive" and "clinging to life" not far from his father's house, Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said at a news conference. It is thought he had been there for 24 hours.
The child is now in hospital receiving care, Koon said, adding he was hopeful he would make a full recovery.
Police are still deciding what further charges to bring against the father.
The search for baby Koah began on Monday after his father took him from his mother's house.
Comer's mother was watching the child and had left her son alone with him briefly, Koon said, when he left abruptly with Koah.
Comer was seen travelling to multiple locations without the baby and was later arrested in Lexington County without Koah. A search party of 100 police and fire department officials were then sent to search for the child, the sheriff said.
He added that when they asked Comer where his son was, he "did not have much to say" about his whereabouts.
Koon said that rescuers searched the woods near Comer's house and saw some "freshly disturbed dirt". As they began to dig, they heard a baby crying - something the sheriff described as "the most joyful sound you ever heard".
"The race was on. Everybody was getting down there trying to get him out," Koon added.
He said the crate was wrapped in a towel that probably provided enough air for Koah to survive for as long as he did, while the cold weather kept him from getting too hot.
"The crate was, probably, I'm guessing about a two-foot [61cm] by two-foot dog crate. So, I think, once that crate hit the ground, he was probably up at least a foot from the top of that crate to the top of the ground," Koon explained.
Of the parents' relationship, the sheriff said there were "obviously some issues". Comer had previously pleaded guilty to domestic violence charges, court records show.
Comer's mother, Patricia Comer, told NBC News that Koah's mother had full custody of him but allowed her to supervise while her son watched him. She said her son had watched the baby before unsupervised without any problems.
"Honestly, I'm his mother, and I never expected this from him," Patricia Comer said.

title: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent relocated after alleged Iranian threats
content:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his Washington DC home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, according to US media reports.
CBS, the BBC's US partner, said the relocation came after a photo of Bessent's home was published in the Wall Street Journal.
Bessent has been at the forefront of efforts to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and a wider economic blockade.
While the exact nature of the threats against Bessent remain unclear, US intelligence has warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans, including US officials.
"After the Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase," a source told CBS.
Georgetown is an affluent part of Washington that is home to a number of government officials and prominent residents.
Those security concerns, the source added, prompted authorities to move Bessent to a military base in the area.
In a statement, a Treasury Department spokesperson said only that Bessent "will not be deterred" by threats and "remains committed" to the US effort to pressure Iran's economy.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
In September, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans.
The New York Times has reported that the Iranian effort includes the targeting of current and former US officials. One source told the newspaper this has "reached a more advanced stage".
Other US officials reportedly on Iran's list of potential targets include former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, former National Security Advisor John Bolton and Mark Milley, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
Milley and Bolton's security teams were taken away by the Trump administration shortly after he returned to office last year.
Bessent is one of a number of administration officials that live on military bases. The White House's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, was moved to a base in late 2025 - before the conflict with Iran began.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both live on military bases, as did former Attorney General Pam Bondi and former intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard.
The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.
In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a blockade targeting Iranian ports.

title: Indonesia's vice president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
content:
Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power.
It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid.
The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.
The aide, Budi Arie, said Gibran's resignation letter was submitted directly to Prabowo on Wednesday. It remains unclear if it has been accepted.
Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.
Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.
Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.
"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.
It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.
Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.
On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi said.
Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.
Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.
His resignation comes as tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.
Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.
In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.
Last week, authorities arrested presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.
Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.
Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.
All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The  free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.

title: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
content:
Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.
Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.
However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.
Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest."
"I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible.
Comments by Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky were less conciliatory. "Right now... a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the US, and on whether Europe comes to its senses," he said.
After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.
The meetings in Abu Dhabi had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.
For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member.
For Moscow, a reworked "security framework" is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion.
Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while the Kremlin's Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system.
That framework would serve as "a new Yalta and Potsdam", Medinsky said, referring to the 1940s summits in which the victorious Allied powers carved up post-war Europe into spheres of influence.
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.
Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin - with whom the EU does not officially communicate - said its delegation had not had any contact with them.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.
Many - particularly in eastern Europe - feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented "if no consensus can be reached among Nato members," a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday.
Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them "added to the format" would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin.
There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted.
Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur "until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues," he added.
Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are essential to its security.

title: Clashes erupt in Barcelona after thousands join Spain general strike
content:
Clashes have broken out between groups of masked men and police in Barcelona after tens of thousands of people took part in Spain's first general strike for 14 years, called by the country's main unions over housing and the high cost of living.
Some 120,000 people joined a demonstration in the capital Madrid and more than 50,000 turned out in Barcelona, where footage showed masked men setting fire to rubbish bins and smashing shop windows as police fired tear gas.
Transport and other public services across Spain faced serious disruption.
Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November.
The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant."
There was a heavy police presence in the centre of Barcelona on Wednesday evening, with officers wearing helmets and riot shields.
Some of the disturbances took place in the Passeig de Gràcia, close to the iconic Plaça de Catalunya in the centre of the city.
Small fires burned in the middle of the streets as bins were set alight. Local media reported that a group of people fired fireworks towards police and looted shops including the Lego store. Protesters were also seen trying to enter the Apple Store.
The BBC spoke to a woman who attended the protests in Barcelona who said it was mostly very peaceful and "joyful".  She said she was there to protest about the housing costs and that "there were a lot of children and old people there."
She was in the area of Las Ramblas in the evening and saw fires in the streets.  "The fires were everywhere, it was very intense," she said.
Earlier in the day there was major disruption around Madrid and Barcelona, with traffic halted on several main roads.
The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices.
"We've completely brought the city to a standstill," a protester in Madrid told Reuters news agency, adding there was widespread support for the general strike. "Everyone's out there, despite the rainy weather; everyone's out on the streets."
Another protester, 37-year-old teacher Olga Domingo, said she was protesting because "the housing situation is outrageous. The current cost of living compared to wages is completely unsustainable".
The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later.
Rental prices in the capital have risen in recent years. The monthly cost of a 50 sq m apartment in Madrid was an average of €1,170 ($1,300; £1,000) in October, according to property portal Idealista, while Spain's average gross monthly salary is about €2,460.
That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, well above the 30% level of affordability often recommended by housing experts and public institutions.
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called snap elections last month after parliament failed to approve his plan for housing reform.
Not since 2012, under the conservative government of Mariano Rajoy, has Spain held general strikes.
And while previous strikes have been problematic for the government in power, this one is different. Sánchez and his ministers have even encouraged workers to down tools and demand affordable housing.

title: Four grizzly bears killed in Canada after fatal attack on mother and daughter
content:
Four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with a fatal attack on a mother and daughter in the Canadian province of British Columbia.
Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going on an afternoon walk in a trail area in Bella Coola.
The British Columbia Conservation Office Service (BCCOS) launched an investigation into their deaths and forensic testing has since confirmed a sow and her three cubs were responsible for the attack.
All four were destroyed "in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines" to protect the public, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said in an update on Tuesday.
"Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added.
The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare".
He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area.
The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found.
"Today, we have learned from the BC Conservation Officer Service members that they have captured and euthanized the bears involved in the recent fatal attack," said Samuel Schooner, Elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, in a statement.
"We would like to thank the BC Conservation Officer Service for their dedication and hard work to resolve this incident. This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack. Our thoughts remain with the victims' families."

title: Schools in Italy, Scotland and Northern Ireland hit by threats in suspected bomb hoax
content:
Some 6,300 schools across Italy and more than 700 in Scotland and Northern Ireland have received bomb threats, according to local authorities.
In Italy a number of buildings were evacuated as a precaution but Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said checks so far had not indicated any evidence of "concrete danger".
"These reports appear rather linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern," she said on Facebook.
Scotland's education secretary Mairi McAllan said there was no risk to the public and specialist cyber-crime officers were working to identify the source of the messages. In Northern Ireland education officials told schools to remain open unless otherwise advised by police.
It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.
"As a parent and as a constituency MSP I understand just how concerning this will be for parents, for pupils, for carers and for school staff," McAllan said.
Scottish police had earlier said that the warnings were "immediately assessed" as hoaxes. However some local authorities confirmed that some schools had been evacuated.
"Our advice is that there is no requirement to evacuate schools or keep children away from education based solely on the content of the emails," Police Scotland said.
Italian officials said a single email appeared to have been sent on Wednesday to the inboxes of 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 state schools, and private schools were unaffected.
The message, said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan", caused alarm in many schools.
The BBC has seen the email sent to Scottish schools which appeared to have similar wording, and also referenced the name Mikhail Andropov, although as leader of a "Red Owl" project.
Italy's Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said the incidents involving Italian schools were probably a "cyber-attack, not a genuine risk", adding that there appeared to be a clear strategy behind the rash of threats in across Europe targeting flights, supermarkets and even hospitals.
Italian airports along with airlines elsewhere in Europe were hit by a series of bomb hoaxes last week that prompted a series of scares, evacuations and widespread disruption.
Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.
On Wednesday one Milan headteacher, Anna Bertato, told Italian media she had checked the email address of the sender online: "It was already classified as spam by a student at a university in Taiwan."
Another Milan headteacher, Massimo Nunzio Barrella, told Adnkronos news agency that he had immediately realised the email was spam when it arrived in his inbox at 08:59 and he decided not to evacuate his school and reassured parents who phoned in.
"The text seemed almost comical," said Barrella, "it was like a message from Martians: 'We have come to annihilate you.' I even had a bit of a laugh."
Although many schools were initially evacuated on Wednesday, the alarm was quickly lifted, and pupils were allowed to return to class. Some parents decided to take their children home for the day, but the majority of schools in Milan did not send their pupils home.
Some 280 school head teachers had already received threats in recent days, according to Italian reports.
In a statement, the head of the central Umbria region Stefania Proietti said "checks conducted so far in Umbrian schools have proved negative, and law enforcement is working rapidly and carefully to verify each report".

title: New Indian mega library rocked by scandal over 'AI-generated books'
content:
An Indian court has ordered an investigation into allegations that a public library in the southern state of Tamil Nadu bought hundreds of books suspected of being generated using AI.
The controversy began after Tamil novelist Perumal Murugan raised concerns about books containing false information and questionable authorship at a newly opened library in Coimbatore city.
The Madras High Court has ordered the state's anti-corruption agency to investigate the purchases and freeze bank accounts linked to a publisher accused of supplying the books.
The state government has blamed the previous Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) party-led administration for buying the books. The DMK denies allegations.
Tamil Nadu's School Education Minister A Rajmohan has described the allegations as potentially "India's first AI scam" and said the investigation would cover purchases at other public libraries across the state.
The case has raised wider questions about the growing use of AI in publishing, where tools can generate entire books quickly and cheaply, but also produce false information and invented references.
It has also highlighted the challenges facing libraries and publishers in checking the authenticity of books as AI-generated content becomes more widespread.
The controversy centres on the Periyar Arivulagam library, built at a cost of about 3bn rupees ($34m; £26m). Named after social reformer Periyar EV Ramasamy, it was inaugurated on 16 October by Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay.
Murugan, whose novels Pyre and One Part Woman have received international recognition, raised concerns after visiting the library last month.
Writing in an online magazine, he alleged that nearly 1,800 books in its Tamil section had been supplied by a little-known publisher called Agal Vilakku Pathippagam.
He said many of the books carried unfamiliar authors' names, unusually high prices and questionable International Standard Book Numbers (ISBNs).
One book cited in the controversy, Naladiyar Vaazhvin Vazhikatti (A Guide to Life through Naladiyar), was reportedly priced at 1,445 rupees for 300 pages.
It describes Naladiyar as a Tamil poet and philosopher, although Naladiyar is a classical Tamil work consisting of 400 four-line verses on morality and ethics.
Another book reportedly attributes the ancient Tamil poem Madurai Kanchi to an incorrect author. It remains unclear whether AI was used to produce any of the disputed books.
Questions have also been raised about a book found at another public library in Madurai which names renowned economist Jean Drèze as its author.
The book, Democracy and People's Rights in the Contemporary World, names renowned economist Jean Drèze as its author and was published by Phoenix Publishing House.
Drèze did not respond to BBC Tamil's request for comment but told The Hindu newspaper earlier this week that he had not written the book, raising concerns that his name may have been used without his permission.
BBC Tamil visited a Chennai address listed by Agal Vilakku and another publisher named in the controversy, Phoenix Publishing House, but found no signs identifying either business.
A woman at the address confirmed that Agal Vilakku operated there. Its proprietor, Mohan, declined to comment, saying the matter was before the courts.

title: Dua Lipa to become first female British headliner at Coachella 2027
content:
Coachella has announced the line-up for its 2027 festival, with Dua Lipa set to be the first solo female British artist to headline.
The Training Season singer is top of Friday's bill for both weekends in April, with psych-rock band Tame Impala headlining the Saturday shows and US singer SZA closing out both Sundays.
The massive festival returns to the California desert on 9 to 11 and 16 to 18 April next year, with more than 100,000 fans expected to attend each day.
Madonna is also set to return to the festival after a surprise appearance alongside this year's headliner Sabrina Carpenter , 20 years on from her first Coachella set.
The Queen of Pop came back with Confessions II, her first album since 2019, earlier this year and had been rumoured to be headlining Glastonbury 2027 before organisers ruled that out.
Swedish pop star Zara Larsson and US singer-songwriter Phoebe Bridgers are also set to perform, as well as Diljit Dosanjh who returns after making history in 2023 by becoming the first Punjabi language singer to perform at the festival.
Blackpink's Jisoo, US star Kehlani, rock band Weezer and Dancing On My Own singer Robyn are also among the artists on the line-up.
The festival will mark a reunion for Dua Lipa and SZA after the pair both headlined Glastonbury in 2024.
During her Pyramid stage set, Dua, who earlier this year married could-be James Bond actor Callum Turner , also brought out Tame Impala frontman Kevin Parker.
She becomes the first British woman to headline Coachella after Charli XCX  performed on the main stage in 2025 before Green Day's headline slot.
During the success of her album Brat, the 365 singer made headlines after being pictured wearing a 'Miss Should Be Headliner' sash following her set.
Green Day appeared to respond with frontman Billie Joe Armstrong wearing a Brat baseball cap during their performance the following weekend.
Other UK artists on the 2027 line-up include EsDeeKid, Chase & Status and Jorja Smith.
Coachella is one of the most high-profile music festivals in the world thanks to its line-up and reputation for attracting a celebrity audience.
Tickets go on sale on Friday.

title: Police helped remove Russell Brand after 'violent incident' at Jemima Goldsmith's home
content:
Police have confirmed they helped Jemima Goldsmith to remove ex-boyfriend Russell Brand from her property in 2014 after she claimed a violent incident took place.
Thames Valley Police said officers were contacted by an alleged victim and went to an address in Oxfordshire on 25 July 2014 but no arrests were made.
They listened to her concerns and gave support, and "also ensured the victim's partner left the address, as per the victim's wishes", the police added in a statement on Wednesday.
Goldsmith, who dated Brand for about a year, wrote on X on Monday that she "had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident" but chose not to press charges.
Brand was jailed for 10-and-a-half years for rape and sexual assault on Monday.
In her post, 52-year-old Goldsmith, who wasn't part of the trial, said she was "in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand's trial" and was "glad and relieved" he had "finally faced justice".
She wrote: "I have had my own personal experience of his violence, coercive control and abuse.
"I had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident."
The Press Association reported that Goldsmith had asked for Brand to leave the property, her wish was then communicated to him by police, and he agreed to leave the house.
Goldsmith added: "I chose not to press charges at the time and not to go public with this, as I was worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children.
"I have neither seen nor spoken to Brand since that period in 2014. Whilst my pain in relation to this, pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact."
She also said she had "assisted the journalists who finally exposed him", and had been willing to testify to his "abusiveness" if they were sued.
TV producer Goldsmith is also the former wife of ex-Pakistani prime minister and cricketer Imran Khan, the daughter of late billionaire entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith and sister of ex-Conservative government minister Zac Goldsmith.

title: Video shows soldier reprimanding Hegseth and advisers at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
content: A US Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier reprimanded Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and a group of his senior advisers Wednesday after some in the group laughed and talked near the solemn memorial following a Veterans Day ceremony. “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times,” the sentinel called out, stopping his patrol to face the group as they departed. Hegseth was standing and taking photos in front of the tomb with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser and deputy assistant Tami Radabaugh after the ceremony held at Arlington National Cemetery for Veterans Day. Some in the group were laughing and chatting after taking photos, prompting the soldier patrolling in front of the Tomb to yell out and correct them. When asked for comment, Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said the “soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.” “The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored—and will always honor—the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe. While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum,” Parnell said. The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is one of the most sacred war memorials in the US, marking the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I. A soldier assigned to The Old Guard, or 3rd Infantry Regiment, has been guarding the tomb around the clock, rain or shine, since 1948. Foreign dignitaries, presidents, public figures and politicians frequently visit the Tomb to pay their respects to American service members. Hegseth and his team were at Arlington National Cemetery for a ceremony that was also attended by President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance. The defense secretary had been under renewed scrutiny and pressure in recent days after articles of impeachment were filed against him by outgoing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie. But in a procedural vote on Tuesday night, the GOP successfully blocked the impeachment process from moving forward, prompting Hegseth and his allies to claim vindication. Hegseth stood accused by Massie of executing unlawful orders, including by waging war in Iran without congressional approval, ignoring laws about minimizing civilian casualties, and directing the Pentagon to carry out extrajudicial killings. In a press conference on Tuesday, Hegseth said the charges amounted to a policy dispute and not high crimes and misdemeanors. President Donald Trump, who also faced criticism for behavior at Arlington National Cemetery when he filmed a campaign video there in 2024, stood by Hegseth leading up to Tuesday’s vote and vowed to continue supporting him moving forward. This story has been updated with additional information.

title: The pendulum can’t stop swinging back and forth in Washington
content: Democrats are celebrating a wave election in which they were handed control of both the House and the Senate. But buyer beware: The pendulum of power is swinging more and more frequently in the United States. In the 100 years between 1900 and 2000, control of the House, Senate or White House changed hands in Washington with relative infrequency, and never in more than two elections in a row. In the 25 years since 2000, the party controlling the White House and/or at least one chamber of Congress changed in all but two US elections. It is an unprecedented period of political turnover in which voters have pulled the lever for some kind of change — either picking a president from a new party or flipping the majority in the House or Senate — nearly every time they’re given the chance in recent years. Voters increasingly complain the country is headed in the wrong direction no matter who is in charge of the executive or the legislative branch. There is bipartisan frustration at a system that feels “rigged,” a perception that cuts across political lines and is driven by income inequality. Many Americans feel left behind and neither party has found the answer, despite promises made every election season. At least one lever of power has flipped between Republicans and Democrats in Washington in each of the last seven elections — the most consecutive power changes going back to before the Civil War. In five of the last seven presidential elections, voters opted for a president from the other party. In the same time period, voters elected a new Senate majority six times and picked a new House majority five times. The only elections this century in which the House, Senate and White House all remained under control of the same party were the only two successful presidential reelection campaigns, for George W. Bush in 2004 and Barack Obama in 2012. Those are also the only times the same party held on to the White House this century. Today’s politicians have come to expect frequent shifts in power. The last four presidents have all assumed office with unified control of Washington and worked as quickly as possible to exploit it. Barack Obama, Donald Trump, Joe Biden and Trump again in his second term all utilized reconciliation to get around the roadblock of the filibuster in the Senate and pass some sort of sweeping agenda item without help from the other party. For Obama, it was the Affordable Care Act. For Trump, it was tax cuts in his first term; in his second, it was a sweeping tax cut and agenda bill that pared back social safety net spending. For Biden, it was the Inflation Reduction Act, which had a lot more to do with clean energy and climate change than it did with reducing inflation. President George W. Bush defied political gravity and picked up House seats after his first two years in office, but that had a lot to do with his popularity after the 9/11 terror attacks. Bush lost the House four years later, after his reelection, when the public had turned on the wars. Bill Clinton lost the House in his first midterm, the 1994 Republican revolution. It was the first time Republicans had gained control of the House since the 1950s. They’ve lost and regained the House twice in the years since. Clinton picked up seats in the 1998 midterm, when the country turned against Republican efforts to impeach him. One way the blue wave of 2026 is different is that Democrats will have a large majority in the House. With potentially 260 or more Democrats, they could end up with the largest majority since the early 1990s, the end of an era in which they routinely had large congressional majorities over the course of decades after World War II. The closest corollary to today in terms of change elections is probably the late 19th century, according to Sarah Binder, a senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution. “It was similarly a period of high partisanship and ideological disagreement,” she said back in 2025. In fact, the 2026 midterm may be compared the most to 1894 , during the second term of Grover Cleveland — the only president besides Trump to serve nonconsecutive terms in the White House. That midterm, when Democrats lost more than 100 seats, came during a period of economic uncertainty and railroad speculation, and the midterm helped usher in a major political realignment. This year will return Democrats to the kind of majority that has not been seen in the House since the early 1990s. A larger realignment also does not seem implausible today as Democrats struggle to reconcile democratic socialists pulling them to the left with majority making moderates who won in red states. For Republicans, Trump’s MAGA coalition feels completely broken at the moment.

title: Biden says he would not have proceeded with campaign had he known he had cancer
content: Former President Joe Biden said in an interview released on Wednesday that his debate performance with Donald Trump in 2024 “was not very consequential” and that he would have not tried to seek a second term had he known he had cancer. The interview with PEOPLE comes ahead of the release of Biden’s presidential memoir, “Promise Me, America,” next week. The July 2024 debate, in which Biden appeared confused and had difficulty articulating his case for another term, eventually led to the president dropping out of the race and endorsing his vice president, Kamala Harris, just 107 days before the 2024 election. His debate performance also prompted his wife, first lady Jill Biden, to think the president was having a stroke. But Biden downplayed its influence in the new interview. “Look, I don’t know anybody who hasn’t made a mistake in a debate,” Biden said in the PEOPLE interview. “To me, it was not very consequential. First of all, I thought there’d be another debate, which there wasn’t. But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn’t another debate, it didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential.” A planned second debate took place in September, but between Harris and Trump. The former president was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer just four months after leaving office. He conceded to having felt “lousy” before knowing about the cancer, and added he would not have attempted to mount another campaign for the White House had he known he was sick. “If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer, I would have resigned. I would’ve not gone forward, because I don’t think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running for (president),” he said. “But that wasn’t the case … I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job.” He said he let the public know of his diagnosis “when we found out” and denied having hid the truth about his health during his presidency. “I didn’t do that,” Biden said. “We let the public know when I found out, when I knew what was going on. I think it’s important for a national leader, as president, to let people know they go through some of the very same things that a lot of American people are going through.” Biden’s book will be released next Tuesday. He has said his cancer will limit his ability to promote it.

title: House Republicans’ middle is disappearing
content: In the painful days after last week’s election disaster, Dave Joyce, a senior Republican from Ohio, delivered a warning to fellow Rep. Jim Jordan as the conservative firebrand sought his vote for party leader. “We can’t double down on stupid,” Joyce recalled telling both Jordan and his unsuccessful challenger, Rep. Steve Scalise, ahead of this week’s leadership race. Joyce is far from an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump. But he — and some like him — are cautioning that they do not want to see their party further embrace the MAGA agenda after one of the party’s biggest wipeouts in decades . “What happened to us was a message, clear and very loud, that people don’t like the way we’re been moving in the wrong direction,” Joyce told CNN. “You can’t lie to people about the things that they feel. They feel it at the pump. They feel it at the grocery store. They feel it in their kids’ education, in the potential for losing their jobs to AI. And we haven’t done anything to address those.” Joyce and other centrist Republicans are urging GOP leaders to forgo scorched-earth attacks on Democrats in place of a real agenda. But in the early, post-election soul-searching, they are in the clear minority of a party that last week elected its most conservative class of members yet. Just days after the election, Republicans chose Jordan , Trump’s prized combatant, to lead them in the new Congress in a landslide vote against establishment-backed Scalise. Then, within hours, all but one Republican blocked a vote that would have triggered an impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth under fierce pressure from the White House. Jordan allies argue he’s more than a rubber stamp for any president and note he has won the support of several more moderate Republicans. Still, lawmakers like Joyce and Rep. Mike Simpson represent the disappearing middle of a decimated Republican Party that, even days after its election drubbing, is showing no daylight between themselves and Trump. “I think what the American people want to see is us working together to resolve problems, not when we bring up crazy shit — or crazy bills opposing stuff. We do need to address the high energy crisis and cost of living, housing,” Simpson, a Republican from Idaho, said. “Like I try to tell people, the Democrats are not the enemy. They are our opposition.” Leaders of the House Freedom Caucus said Wednesday that Republicans lost because they didn’t go far enough in their agenda, such as a border crackdown bill or Trump’s marquee voting bill that languished in the Senate. “Nobody listened to us,” Rep. Scott Perry, a GOP hardliner who lost a House battleground seat in Pennsylvania, declared. “It’s not because we didn’t do enough liberal things that we had the result last Tuesday. It’s because we didn’t deliver on the things that we told America we were going to do.” Many of those ultraconservative Republicans are now pushing for a last-gasp policy package in the final weeks that would codify some of Trump’s hardline border policies, as well as “at least $1 trillion” in spending cuts from government programs. The future of the GOP is far from settled, with a nasty 2028 presidential primary cycle just ahead. But in a sign of how the party plans to handle Trump’s remaining two years in power, almost no one is publicly blaming the president in their election loss. “If you look at our conference; we’re a significantly more conservative conference than what we were coming into this,” Rep. Brian Mast of Florida, a strong Jordan ally, told CNN when asked about the direction the party would take post-election. Asked if he believed Republicans needed to moderate their political stances to win back voters next cycle, Mast replied: “Our moderation is this: the Constitution is our moderation. The Constitution should pull people in from the left and the right, and I think we do a better job of being guided by the Constitution on the right, and that will be our moderation.” Most of the now-ousted members belonged to groups like the centrist Republican Governance Group, which lost nearly half of its roughly 50 members. Another, the Problem Solvers Caucus, lost 13 of its 19 GOP members, including its GOP co-leader. Put another way: Of the 120 Republicans who refused to challenge the 2020 election results as Trump demanded, only about two dozen remain. Rep. Nick LaLota, a Long Island Republican, is another centrist eager to work with Democrats next year on issues like immigration reform. Asked what lessons Trump should take away from the election, LaLota said he agreed with Trump’s own post-election reflections in a recent “60 Minutes” interview that his deportation policy might have been “too tough” and that it was “bad messaging, maybe by me.” LaLota, who is seeking to take over the mantle of the Republican Governance Group from Joyce, said his own tactics wouldn’t change. “I’ll fight for my common-sense conservative values. But I’m also willing to negotiate and compromise – I don’t view those as bad words,” he said.

title: Senior Reform UK official quits as questions over vetting failures continue
content: Reform UK’s general secretary has left the role as Nigel Farage’s party continues to face turmoil over questions about vetting failures and professionalisation. The departure of Tom Waterhouse comes after Reform UK’s leader on Hampshire county council, George Madgwick, was charged with 12 counts of rape and one of distributing indecent images of a child. Waterhouse, a public affairs executive who previously worked in the world of Westminster thinktanks and for the crown estate, was recruited in August last year. Labour described him as Reform’s “latest fall guy” for problems in the party. A Reform UK spokesperson said: “Tom Waterhouse has left his role with Reform UK. The party leader has now appointed an interim general secretary.” Waterhouse’s departure will be a blow to Reform’s drive towards professionalisation, a project of which he had been at the centre. He had been involved in a big recruitment push, bankrolled by wealthy donors, and in the selection of candidates for a future general election. Waterhouse had also been involved in Reform’s internal investigation into two of its senior officials, James Orr and Dan Jukes, alongside Adam Richardson, the party’s legal secretary and a longstanding associate of Farage. Their investigation cleared Orr and Jukes of breaking laws that ban foreign donations, despite the matter remaining under police investigation. However, the recent case of Madgwick severely embarrassed the party and once again brought the question of Reform’s candidate vetting process into the spotlight. That process is now run by Paul Nuttall, the party’s deputy chair and a former Ukip leader, but Waterhouse’s departure reflects continuing organisational turmoil at Reform. Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said: “As the scandals pile up for Reform, everyone is being forced to take the blame except Nigel Farage. Their general secretary is the latest fall guy, but we all know nobody in Reform makes a decision without Farage’s approval. “Farage is yet to come clean on what he knew about the arrest of his senior campaign manager and leader in Hampshire, who is now facing 35 very serious charges. And he tried to cover up a secret £5m ‘gift’ from a crypto billionaire.” Sign up to Breaking News UK Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox after newsletter promotion The Reform leader has not concealed his unhappiness at continued failures in candidate vetting and other matters. “I wasn’t very happy,” Farage said when asked why Madgwick, who was arrested in January over several alleged sexual offences, was still in his role nearly 10 months later. Madgwick denies any wrongdoing. Farage last month blamed “staff incompetence” for a poor turnout and a half-empty hall during a Reform UK economic policy launch event in London. Staff at Reform’s Millbank HQ were informed on Wednesday that Waterhouse was leaving. He is one of a number of figures seen as an asset to Reform’s push for power who have recently parted ways with the party or been sidelined. Tim Montgomerie , a high-profile activist who defected from the Conservatives, was suspended in August after he criticised Farage’s decision not to attend the count when he won the Clacton byelection.

title: All Kemi had at PMQs was jokes … and unfunny jokes at that
content: W ell, there was one person at least who thought Kemi Badenoch had absolutely nailed it at this week’s prime minister’s questions. And that person was Kemi Badenoch. She could not have been more pleased with herself if she had tried. No one laughed louder and longer at her own jokes than she did. No one admired her laser focus as much as she did. Kemi is the paid up chief executive of her own fanclub. As for the rest of her Tory MPs – aside from Chris Philp, who is basically a parasitic homunculus – they weren’t quite so convinced by Kemi’s performance. She had been so entranced with her one-liners, she had forgotten to ask any serious questions. And never forget how low the gag bar is in the Commons. What passes as a joke at PMQs wouldn’t even register as humour in normal conversation. Wouldn’t even elicit the groan that comes from the recognition of a gag format. Maybe Kemi was just having a bad day. Had woken up and realised she didn’t have any questions for the prime minister and had decided to busk it instead. Maybe she was so carried away with the excitement of the Tories no longer being in third place in the opinion polls – mainly because Reform have tanked rather than any Conservative surge – that she decided to give herself a day off. Or maybe she’s stalled somewhat. Having found she could get under Keir Starmer’s skin, she merely bounces off Andy Burnham’s. Compared with Kemi, Andy looks and sounds like a normal person. The session began with Kemi trying to make fun of Labour’s as-yet-unpublished – possibly even unwritten – 10-year plan. Where was it, she asked. Burnham had a ready answer . It would be presented in the Commons before Christmas. Answers don’t come much more straight than that. Kemi looked almost disappointed. She was sure the 10-year plan had been kicked into the long grass. On Tuesday she had joked it would be a nine-year plan by the time it was published. Now the joke was on her. It was as though Kemi was just going through a set list of topics from which she could riff. As if she was a standup comedian doing improv. Next in her sights came the budget. Not that she had any real observation to make about it. But she did have a gag and that was all that mattered. It was the “do nothing” budget. Kemi cracked herself up at that. Turning to the stony faces behind her for approval. You know, the “do nothing” budget? Get it? Er … yes. But it wasn’t funny the first time. Burnham meanwhile seemed rather surprised by the turn of events. He had been expecting something rather more taxing. Something less lightweight. He doesn’t really get Kemi’s obsession with panto. Mind you, it’s only going to get worse as we get closer and closer to the Christmas season. It won’t be long before Kemi shouts out: “He’s behind you” and convulses on the floor with laughter. So Andy just continued to do his Mr Congeniality act. The career politician with the priceless ability to sound as if he isn’t a career politician. Someone you are inclined to like and trust on sight. The bedside manner of a doctor who can somehow make you feel better about yourself when telling you your illness has become terminal. The sort of person who you feel guilty about for not having responded to treatment. By now Kemi was about halfway through her routine and had decided it was time to talk about the Rosebank oilfield. Might as well. Hadn’t mentioned it for a week or so. Not that she had anything new to say, but that wasn’t going to stop her. The old ones are … the old ones. Andy merely replied that it was the Tories who had drawn up the licence and that Labour had already given the go-ahead to Jackdaw. Rosebank would be ready when it was ready. It wasn’t as if it was particularly time sensitive. For reasons best known to herself, Kemi now thought it was time for a Russell Brand gag at Ed Miliband’s expense. On Tuesday, Kemi had made a point of refusing to do this. Of being the grownup when invited by a rightwing journalist to score points over Labour at a press conference. She wasn’t going to do this, she said. It was both disrespectful to Brand’s victims and wrong to attack politicians from whatever party for associations they had made before a person’s crimes were in the public domain. It had been a strange moment. One that possibly marked Kemi out as grown-up potential. Sign up to Breaking News UK Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox after newsletter promotion It turned out to be an aberration. Tuesday was Tuesday. Wednesday was another day. The victims had had more than enough time now. And who couldn’t resist the opportunity of taking a pop at Ed Mil? If Kemi had any sense of history, she would have remembered that Margaret Thatcher had once lionised Jimmy Savile. Most politicians have done things they regret. Miliband had appeared to be having second thoughts about meeting Brand even as he was interviewing him. The exchanges ended with Kemi listing some of her complaints against Labour and asking whether the Labour MPs really thought it had been worth replacing Starmer with Burnham. This was not just unfunny, it was totally half witted. Because even her own backbenchers can see that Labour MPs are completely blissed out with Andy. He might be more vibes than delivery at the moment, but you can’t argue with the numbers. Labour are a good six to eight points ahead of the Tories in the polls. Something that was unimaginable when Keir had been removed in July. Voters seem to like him. They feel he is honest and respond to his positivity. They accept that the Tories damaged the economy and are willing to give him time to put things right. And compared with Kemi, Burnham looks and sounds like a leader. Someone who can put party politics to one side when needed. Not something you can say about Kemi at this PMQs. All she had was jokes. And the jokes weren’t even that funny.
